newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: France seen dropping opposition to Annan in UN job.
newsitem.headline: France seen dropping opposition to Annan in UN job.

text.p: Diplomats expressed growing optimism on Friday that France would drop its opposition to the nomination of Kofi Annan of Ghana to be the next U.N. secretary-general.

Several members of the Security Council and senior U.N. officials said off the record they were fairly sure an unofficial poll scheduled for later in the day would give Annan, the U.N. undersecretary-general for peacekeeping, the votes of all 15 council members.
One member said the only uncertainty was whether the official vote would come late on Friday or be postponed until next Monday.
A French diplomat would say only: "We are working to seek consensus."

The 58-year-old Annan, a soft-spoken career U.N. official, obtained 14 votes in the most recent unofficial poll on Thursday, with France the only holdout. The five permanent council members -- the United States, Russia, Britain, China and France -- have the power of veto in any formal voting.
Annan's 14-1 showing -- his best in seven unofficial polls so far -- equalled the vote obtained by incumbent Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali in a formal council vote on Nov. 19.

The 74-year-old Egyptian diplomat, whose current five-year term expires on Dec. 31, was the only candidate on that occasion but was vetoed by the United States, which insists the United Nations needs new leadership to introduce reforms.

Boutros-Ghali suspended his candidacy on Dec. 4 but did not definitively withdraw, and four other African hopefuls then entered the race, including Annan, who led consistently on each of the unofficial ballots.
France supported Boutros-Ghali and backed candidates from French-speaking African countries since he stepped down.

Annan's closest rival in the balloting has been Amara Essy, the foreign minister of the Ivory Coast and the 1994-95 U.N. General Assembly president. He received seven votes in unofficial polling on Thursday, with two permanent members opposing him, the United States and Britain.

The two other candidates, who have consistently fallen far short of the minimum of nine votes needed, are Ahmedou Ould-Abdallah, a former foreign minister of Mauritania and former U.N. envoy for Burundi; and Hamid Algabid, a former prime minister of Niger and currently secretary-general of the Organisation of the Islamic Conference.

Africa has been given priority up to now in putting forward candidates for the top U.N. post on grounds that if Boutros-Ghali is denied the second term usually accorded a secretary-general he should be succeeded by another African.
But if France persisted in opposing Annan the contest could be thrown open to candidates from other regions.
